Key supportive findings: bilateral, hyperpigmented verrucous plaques confined to nipples/areolae; short history but no erythema, discharge, or lymphadenopathy; and skin-biopsy showing hyperkeratosis and papillomatosis. Those histologic features classically occur in nevoid (or idiopathic) hyperkeratosis of the nipple and areola (HNA), which typically presents as hyperpigmented, verrucous/velvety thickening of the nipple–areolar complex and can be bilateral.

Important differentials and why they are less likely:
- Mammary Paget disease: usually unilateral, eczematous/crusted/eroded nipple with Paget cells on histology (not just hyperkeratosis/papillomatosis).

- Acanthosis nigricans: histology overlaps (papillomatosis, hyperkeratosis) but typically involves multiple intertriginous sites and has a velvety rather than verrucous appearance and is often diffuse.

Given the anatomic localization, bilateral involvement, clinical appearance, and matching histopathology, idiopathic/nevoid hyperkeratosis of the nipple and areola is the single most likely diagnosis.

### Proposed Diagnosis ###
Nevoid (idiopathic) hyperkeratosis of the nipple and areola (hyperkeratosis of the nipple and areola).

[THOUGHT] The clinical presentation (bilateral, hyperpigmented verrucous plaques of the nipples/areolae) and the initial biopsy showing hyperkeratosis and papillomatosis are consistent with nevoid/idiopathic hyperkeratosis of the nipple and areola (NHNA). A deeper excisional specimen was obtained and documented as adequate, with explicit negative findings for Paget (no large pale/Paget cells), no dermal invasion/atypia, and “normal” immunohistochemistry (CK7, EMA, CEA, HER2) and mucin stains — findings that effectively exclude Paget disease of the nipple, which is the principal malignancy to rule out for this presentation. Bilaterality further lowers the probability of Paget-related underlying carcinoma. 

Red flags / missing elements: advanced patient age (>60) increases baseline malignancy risk and ordinarily mandates breast imaging (diagnostic mammogram ± targeted ultrasound) to exclude an underlying carcinoma; however, the excisional biopsy plus negative IHC/mucin stains provides strong pathologic evidence against Paget disease. There is incomplete documentation of imaging (ordered but not performed/available) and some patient uncertainty about test recall, but the pathology entries indicate an adequately sampled negative excisional biopsy.

Given the available pathology showing adequate depth, absence of Paget cells or atypia, and negative IHC/mucin stains, the diagnosis of nevoid (idiopathic) hyperkeratosis of the nipple and areola is sufficiently supported.
